events.title: Rise of Elamite Civilization
events.description: The Elamite civilization emerged in southwestern Iran, one of the world's oldest civilizations. The Elamites developed a unique writing system and urban culture, with Susa as the political and commercial center. Elam had close interactions with Mesopotamian civilizations, profoundly influencing Persian culture.

events.title: Proto-Elamite Kingdom
events.description: The Proto-Elamite Kingdom was established, ruling southwestern Iran. The Elamites cooperated and competed with the Sumerians, playing an important role in Mesopotamia. Elamite art, architecture, and administrative systems reached high development.

events.title: Aryan Migration
events.description: Indo-European Aryan tribes migrated from Central Asia to the Iranian plateau. These tribes, including the Medes and Persians, brought horses, chariots, and new social organization. The name 'Iran' derives from 'Land of the Aryans.' This migration laid the foundation for Persian civilization.

events.title: Birth of Zoroaster
events.description: The prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) was born, founding Zoroastrianism. This religion advocated dualism of good and evil, worshiping Ahura Mazda (God of Light). Zoroastrianism became the Persian Empire's state religion, profoundly influencing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

events.title: Median Kingdom Founded
events.description: The Medes established a kingdom in northwestern Iran, with capital at Ecbatana. The Median Kingdom allied with Babylon to overthrow the Assyrian Empire, becoming a major power in the ancient Near East. The Median Kingdom laid the foundation for the later Persian Empire.

events.title: Medes Destroy Assyria
events.description: Median King Cyaxares and Babylonian forces captured Nineveh, destroying the mighty Assyrian Empire. This victory made Media the strongest state in the Near East, controlling vast territory from Anatolia to the Iranian plateau.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Founds Persian Empire
events.description: Persian king Cyrus II (Cyrus the Great) overthrew the Median Kingdom, establishing the Achaemenid Dynasty, the First Persian Empire. Cyrus was renowned for his tolerance, allowing conquered peoples to maintain their culture and religion. He built the ancient world's largest empire.

events.title: Conquest of Babylon
events.description: Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon, freed captive Jews, and allowed them to return to Jerusalem to rebuild the Temple. This benevolent act earned Cyrus the title 'Anointed One' in the Bible. The Cyrus Cylinder, recording his tolerance policy, is considered an early human rights declaration.

events.title: Cyrus Dies in Battle
events.description: Cyrus the Great died in battle against the Massagetae. His son Cambyses II succeeded him. Cyrus is considered the greatest ruler in Persian history; his tomb at Pasargadae is still revered today.

events.title: Darius I Ascends
events.description: Darius I became king after a coup, suppressed nationwide rebellions, and consolidated imperial rule. He divided the empire into 20 satrapies, establishing efficient administrative and postal systems. Darius brought the Persian Empire to its zenith, with territory from the Indus to the Danube.

events.title: Construction of Persepolis
events.description: Darius I began building Persepolis as the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Dynasty. This magnificent palace complex showcased the pinnacle of Persian architecture, art, and multicultural character. Persepolis reliefs depicted various nations paying tribute to the Persian king, symbolizing the empire's universality.

events.title: Suppression of Ionian Revolt
events.description: Greek cities in Ionia (Asia Minor) revolted against Persian rule, with support from Athens. Darius suppressed the revolt but decided to punish Athens, triggering the Greco-Persian Wars.

events.title: Battle of Marathon
events.description: Darius sent an expedition to attack Athens but was defeated at the Battle of Marathon by Athenian forces. This was the Persian Empire's first major military setback, boosting Greek morale and becoming a pivotal battle in Western civilization.

events.title: Xerxes Invades Greece
events.description: Darius's son Xerxes I led a massive army to invade Greece. Persian forces broke through Spartan defenses at Thermopylae and burned Athens. However, the Persian navy was crushed at the Battle of Salamis by the Greek fleet. Xerxes withdrew, and Persian expansion was thwarted.

events.title: Alexander Conquers Persia
events.description: Macedonian Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at the Battle of Gaugamela, conquering the Persian Empire. Alexander burned Persepolis; the Achaemenid Dynasty fell. Persia entered the Hellenistic period, where Greek and Persian cultures merged.

events.title: Seleucid Dynasty Founded
events.description: Seleucus I, one of Alexander's generals, established the Seleucid Empire, ruling vast territories including Iran. The Seleucids promoted Hellenization, but Persian traditions persisted. This period saw frequent cultural exchanges between East and West.

events.title: Parthian Empire Rises
events.description: The Parthians, an Iranian nomadic tribe, established an empire in northeastern Iran, gradually expanding westward. The Parthians adopted Persian political traditions while resisting Hellenistic influence. The Parthian Empire became a major power bridging East and West.

events.title: Parthians Conquer Mesopotamia
events.description: Parthian King Mithridates I conquered Mesopotamia from the Seleucids, making Ctesiphon the capital. Parthia controlled the Silk Road, profiting from East-West trade. The Parthian Empire reached its zenith.

events.title: Battle of Carrhae
events.description: Parthian forces crushed a Roman army at Carrhae led by Crassus, killing the triumvir. This victory demonstrated Parthian military might, with heavy cavalry becoming Rome's nightmare. The Parthian-Roman rivalry dominated the ancient Near East for centuries.

events.title: Sasanian Dynasty Founded
events.description: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthian Dynasty, establishing the Sasanian Dynasty, the Second Persian Empire. The Sasanians revived Persian traditions, making Zoroastrianism the state religion. Sasanian Persia became the Byzantine Empire's main rival, ruling Iran for 400 years.

events.title: Capture of Roman Emperor Valerian
events.description: Sasanian King Shapur I defeated and captured Roman Emperor Valerian, the greatest humiliation in Roman history. Shapur celebrated this victory on rock reliefs, demonstrating Sasanian power. This event shocked the Roman world.

events.title: Reign of Khosrow I
events.description: Khosrow I (Anushirvan the Just) ruled, bringing Sasanian Persia to its golden age. He reformed taxation, promoted learning, and patronized arts and sciences. Greek, Indian, and Chinese knowledge was translated into Persian. Khosrow was renowned for his justice and wisdom.

events.title: Persian-Byzantine Wars
events.description: The Sasanian-Byzantine Wars escalated. Sasanian King Khosrow II briefly conquered Syria, Palestine, and Egypt, reaching Constantinople's gates. However, Byzantine Emperor Heraclius counterattacked, invading Persia. This exhaustive war weakened both empires, paving the way for Arab conquest.

events.title: Battle of Qadisiyyah
events.description: Arab Muslim forces defeated the Sasanian army at the Battle of Qadisiyyah, conquering Mesopotamia. This marked a turning point in the Muslim conquest of Persia. The Sasanian capital Ctesiphon fell soon after.

events.title: Battle of Nihavand and Sasanian Fall
events.description: Arab forces decisively defeated Persian armies at Nihavand; the last Sasanian king Yazdegerd III fled. Yazdegerd was killed in 651; the Sasanian Dynasty ended. Persia was conquered by Arabs, gradually Islamized, but retained unique cultural identity.

events.title: Umayyad Rule
events.description: Persia came under Umayyad Caliphate rule. Though conquered, Persians retained cultural traditions and gradually embraced Islam. Persian scholars, administrators, and merchants played important roles in the Islamic world.

events.title: Abbasid Revolution
events.description: The Abbasid Revolution overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate. Persians played a key role in this revolution. The Abbasids moved the capital to Baghdad, near Persia. Persian culture, administration, and learning profoundly influenced the Abbasid Caliphate.

events.title: Tahirid Dynasty Independence
events.description: The Tahirid Dynasty achieved de facto independence in eastern Iran while nominally recognizing the Abbasid caliph. This marked the beginning of Iranian dynastic revival during the Islamic period.

events.title: Saffarid Dynasty Rises
events.description: The Saffarids established a dynasty in Sistan (eastern Iran). Though short-lived, the Saffarids represented Persian resistance to Arab dominance and promoted Persian language and culture.

events.title: Samanid Golden Age
events.description: The Samanid Dynasty ruled Khorasan and Transoxiana, bringing a Persian cultural renaissance. The Samanids patronized Persian literature; Ferdowsi's Shahnameh was composed in this era. Persian language revived as a literary language.

events.title: Ghaznavid Dynasty
events.description: The Ghaznavids ruled from eastern Iran to northern India. Though Turkic, they patronized Persian culture and literature. Ferdowsi dedicated the Shahnameh to Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni.

events.title: Seljuk Empire Rises
events.description: The Seljuk Turks conquered Iran, establishing a vast empire from Central Asia to Anatolia. The Seljuks adopted Persian administrative systems and culture. Persian viziers like Nizam al-Mulk wielded great power.

events.title: Nizam al-Mulk Reforms
events.description: Persian vizier Nizam al-Mulk served the Seljuk Empire, implementing effective reforms. He established the Nizamiyya schools, promoting Islamic learning. His governance manual 'Book of Government' influenced Islamic political thought.

events.title: Mongol Invasion
events.description: Genghis Khan's Mongol armies invaded Iran, causing unprecedented destruction. Cities like Nishapur and Rey were razed; millions perished. The Mongol invasion devastated Iranian civilization but Persian culture eventually influenced Mongol rulers.

events.title: Hulagu Establishes Ilkhanate
events.description: Hulagu Khan, Genghis's grandson, established the Ilkhanate in Iran. The Ilkhans gradually adopted Islam and Persian culture. Despite Mongol rule, Persian remained the administrative and literary language.

events.title: Ghazan Khan's Reforms
events.description: Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam and implemented comprehensive reforms. He stabilized currency, standardized taxation, and restored agriculture. Under Ghazan's rule, Persian economy and culture recovered. His vizier Rashid al-Din compiled the Jami' al-tawarikh (Compendium of Chronicles), recording world history.

events.title: Timurid Empire
events.description: Timur (Tamerlane) conquered Iran, establishing the Timurid Empire. Though devastating in conquest, Timur and his successors patronized Persian art, literature, and architecture. The Timurid period saw brilliant cultural achievements.

events.title: Turkmen Tribal Confederations
events.description: After Timur's death, Iran fragmented into Turkmen tribal confederations (Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu). Political fragmentation persisted until Safavid unification.

events.title: Safavid Dynasty Founded
events.description: Ismail I established the Safavid Dynasty, unified Iran, and made Tabriz the capital. He declared Twelver Shi'ism the state religion, opposing the Sunni Ottoman Empire. This decision shaped modern Iran's religious identity, making Iran the Shi'a heartland.

events.title: Reign of Abbas I the Great
events.description: Abbas I was the greatest Safavid monarch. He modernized the military, recovered lost territories, and moved the capital to Isfahan. Abbas built magnificent mosques and palaces, making Isfahan 'Half the World.' His reign was Persia's golden age.

events.title: Persian-Ottoman Wars
events.description: Abbas I waged war against the Ottomans, recovering Azerbaijan, Iraq, and Kurdistan. Persian forces, using firearms and new tactics, defeated Ottoman armies repeatedly. The 1618 peace treaty restored Safavid's early territories.

events.title: Afghan Invasion and Safavid Decline
events.description: Afghan Ghilzai tribes invaded, besieged and captured Isfahan; the Safavid Dynasty collapsed. Invaders killed thousands of Persians and destroyed cities. Iran descended into chaos with warlord fragmentation. This was a dark period in Iranian history.

events.title: Nader Shah Founds Afsharid Dynasty
events.description: Military commander Nader Shah overthrew Safavid remnants, proclaimed himself king, and founded the Afsharid Dynasty. He expelled Afghans, conquered Afghanistan and northern India, sacking Delhi in 1739. Nader Shah rebuilt Persian military power but ruled brutally.

events.title: Zand Dynasty Founded
events.description: After Nader Shah's assassination, Karim Khan Zand founded the Zand Dynasty, with capital at Shiraz. Karim Khan was a benevolent ruler committed to peace and prosperity. He lowered taxes, encouraged trade, and built monuments. But the dynasty fell into civil war after his death.

events.title: Qajar Dynasty Founded
events.description: Agha Mohammad Khan defeated the Zand Dynasty, establishing the Qajar Dynasty with Tehran as capital. The Qajars ruled Iran until 1925, but this period saw Iran weakened, facing pressure from Russian and British aggression.

events.title: First Perso-Russian War
events.description: Russia invaded the Caucasus, sparking war with Persia. The 1813 Treaty of Gulistan forced Persia to cede vast Caucasian territories including Georgia, Baku, and Dagestan. This marked the beginning of Persian territorial losses.

events.title: Second Perso-Russian War
events.description: Persia attempted to recover lost lands but was defeated again by Russia. The 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay cost Persia Armenia and Azerbaijan, plus massive reparations. This humiliating treaty marked Persia's semi-colonial status.

events.title: Reign of Naser al-Din Shah
events.description: Naser al-Din Shah ruled for 48 years. He attempted to modernize Iran, introducing Western technology and institutions. But reforms were limited; corruption was severe. To balance Russian-British influence, he sold concessions to foreigners, causing popular discontent. He was assassinated in 1896.

events.title: Reuter Concession Incident
events.description: Naser al-Din Shah granted Baron de Reuter nearly all economic privileges, sparking nationwide protests. The ulama (religious scholars) led opposition; the Shah was forced to cancel the concession. This demonstrated religious institutions' power in Iranian politics.

events.title: Tobacco Protest Movement
events.description: The Shah granted British companies tobacco monopoly, triggering nationwide protests. A Shi'a leader issued a fatwa banning tobacco use; even the Shah's wives joined the boycott. The government was forced to cancel the concession. This movement showed the power of people and ulama united.

events.title: Constitutional Revolution
events.description: Popular uprising forced Mozaffar ad-Din Shah to agree to establish a parliament and draft a constitution. The first Majlis (parliament) convened in 1906, passing a constitution limiting monarchical power. This was Iran's first constitutional attempt, initiating modern political change.

events.title: Anglo-Russian Convention Partitions Iran
events.description: Britain and Russia signed the Anglo-Russian Convention, dividing Iran into spheres of influence: Russia controlled the north, Britain the southeast, with a neutral buffer zone. This agreement ignored Iranian sovereignty, making Iran an Anglo-Russian battleground.

events.title: Oil Discovered
events.description: Britain discovered the Middle East's first major oil field in Khuzestan. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company (later Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, BP's predecessor) began extraction. Oil changed Iran's economy and geopolitical status, but most profits went to Britain.

events.title: Reza Khan's Coup
events.description: Cossack Brigade commander Reza Khan launched a coup with British support, quickly controlling the government. He served as War Minister then Prime Minister, promoting modernization and centralization. In 1925 he deposed the last Qajar Shah and founded the Pahlavi Dynasty.

events.title: Pahlavi Dynasty Founded
events.description: Parliament deposed the Qajar Dynasty, electing Reza Khan as the new Shah, founding the Pahlavi Dynasty. Reza Khan took the name Reza Shah Pahlavi, beginning ambitious modernization programs modeled after Turkey's Kemalist reforms.

events.title: Persia Renamed Iran
events.description: Reza Shah officially changed the country's name from 'Persia' to 'Iran,' emphasizing the nation's Aryan heritage. 'Iran' means 'Land of the Aryans' in Persian. This renaming reflected nationalist trends.

events.title: Allied Invasion and Reza Shah's Abdication
events.description: During WWII, Britain and the USSR, fearing Iran's pro-German leanings, jointly invaded Iran. Reza Shah was forced to abdicate and exiled to South Africa. His 22-year-old son Mohammad Reza succeeded him. Iran became a corridor for supplying aid to the USSR.

events.title: Mossadegh's Oil Nationalization
events.description: Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh pushed parliament to pass oil nationalization, taking the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company into state ownership. This bold move gained enthusiastic public support but triggered British economic sanctions and international isolation. Mossadegh became a Third World anti-colonial symbol.

events.title: Mossadegh Coup (Operation Ajax)
events.description: In a CIA and MI6-orchestrated coup, Mossadegh was overthrown, the Shah's power consolidated. This coup ended Iran's democratic attempt, making the Shah a dictator. The coup's legacy affects Iran today, being the root of US-Iran relations deterioration.

events.title: White Revolution
events.description: The Shah launched the 'White Revolution,' implementing land reform, women's suffrage, and industrialization. But reforms angered landlords and clerics, facing opposition. Ayatollah Khomeini publicly criticized the Shah, was arrested then exiled. The White Revolution sowed seeds of Islamic Revolution.

events.title: 2500th Anniversary Celebration
events.description: The Shah held a lavish celebration at Persepolis for the 2,500th anniversary of the Persian Empire, inviting world leaders. The ceremony cost hundreds of millions of dollars, showcasing Iran's glorious history. But public resentment at the Shah's extravagance grew; this celebration became a revolution precursor.

events.title: Oil Crisis and Economic Boom
events.description: The first oil crisis caused oil prices to skyrocket; Iran's oil revenue surged. The Shah used oil wealth for massive military purchases and industrialization. But rapid development triggered inflation, unequal wealth distribution, rampant corruption, and intensified social contradictions.

events.title: Islamic Revolution Begins
events.description: Qom theology students protested government attacks on Khomeini, were suppressed, sparking nationwide demonstrations. Memorial services every 40 days evolved into anti-Shah movements. People from all walks joined protests demanding the Shah step down. Revolutionary waves swept the nation.

events.title: Black Friday
events.description: On September 8 (Friday), thousands of protesters in Tehran were shot by troops; hundreds died. This massacre enraged the public; demonstrations escalated. The Shah regime's legitimacy collapsed; revolution became irreversible.

events.title: Shah's Exile
events.description: Facing nationwide protests and wavering military, Mohammad Reza Shah fled Iran, nominally for 'vacation.' He never returned, dying in Egypt. The Shah's departure marked the end of the Pahlavi Dynasty and 2,500 years of Persian monarchy.

events.title: Khomeini Returns to Iran
events.description: Ayatollah Khomeini returned to Tehran from Paris after 15 years of exile, welcomed by millions. He declared the Shah's government illegitimate, calling for an Islamic government. The revolution entered its final stage.

events.title: Islamic Republic Established
events.description: Following a referendum, 98% of voters approved establishing the Islamic Republic. Khomeini became Supreme Leader, holding power beyond president and parliament. The new constitution established the principle of Velayat-e Faqih (Guardianship of the Jurist), giving religious leaders final decision-making authority.

events.title: US Embassy Hostage Crisis
events.description: Iranian students seized the US Embassy, holding 52 American diplomats hostage for 444 days. They demanded the US extradite the Shah for trial. The hostage crisis led to US-Iran severing relations, with hostility continuing today. This event shaped Iran's anti-American image.

events.title: Iran-Iraq War
events.description: Iraqi Saddam Hussein invaded Iran, trying to seize Khuzestan oil region during revolutionary chaos. The war lasted 8 years, causing a million casualties and trillions in economic losses. Though Iran held territory, it paid a heavy price. The war galvanized nationalism, consolidating the revolutionary regime.

events.title: Ceasefire Acceptance and War's End
events.description: Khomeini accepted the UN ceasefire resolution, ending the Iran-Iraq War. He described this decision as 'more painful than drinking poison.' The war ended in stalemate, both sides exhausted. Iran entered post-war reconstruction but economic difficulties and international isolation continued.

events.title: Khomeini's Death
events.description: Islamic Revolution leader Ayatollah Khomeini died aged 86. His funeral attracted millions of mourners. Khomeini changed Iran and Middle East history's trajectory. Ali Khamenei succeeded as Supreme Leader, Rafsanjani elected president.

events.title: Rafsanjani Reconstruction Period
events.description: President Rafsanjani pursued pragmatic policies, rebuilding the post-war economy and improving relations with the West. But reforms were obstructed by conservatives; economic recovery was slow. Iran's foreign policy slightly eased, but relations with the US remained tense.

events.title: Khatami Elected President
events.description: Reformist Mohammad Khatami was elected president by a landslide, proposing 'Dialogue Among Civilizations' and rule of law. Khatami's government relaxed social controls, expanded freedom of expression, and improved relations with the West. But reforms were resisted by conservatives and Supreme Leader Khamenei.

events.title: Student Demonstrations
events.description: Tehran University students protested newspaper closures, were violently suppressed by militias. Demonstrations spread nationwide, the largest protests since the revolution. Conservatives crushed the protests; the reform movement suffered setbacks. This highlighted the power struggle between reformists and conservatives.

events.title: Listed as 'Axis of Evil'
events.description: US President Bush labeled Iran, along with Iraq and North Korea, as the 'Axis of Evil' in his State of the Union address, accusing Iran of supporting terrorism and developing weapons of mass destruction. This rhetoric worsened US-Iran relations and increased regional tensions.

events.title: Bam Earthquake
events.description: On December 26, a 6.6 magnitude earthquake struck Bam, killing about 30,000 and almost completely destroying the ancient city. International aid was provided, briefly improving Iran-West relations. But humanitarian cooperation didn't translate into political reconciliation.

events.title: Ahmadinejad Elected President
events.description: Conservative Mahmoud Ahmadinejad defeated former President Rafsanjani to become president. Ahmadinejad took a hardline anti-American stance, advanced the nuclear program, and denied the Holocaust, triggering international condemnation. His populist policies gained lower-class support but exacerbated economic problems.

events.title: Nuclear Crisis Escalates
events.description: Iran resumed uranium enrichment; the UN Security Council passed sanctions resolutions. Iran insisted its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes, but the West suspected nuclear weapons development. The nuclear issue became the focal point of Iran-West confrontation, with sanctions continuously escalating.

events.title: Green Movement
events.description: After presidential election results were announced, the opposition alleged fraud. Millions took to the streets protesting, called the 'Green Movement.' The government violently suppressed demonstrations, arresting dissidents. Though crushed, the Green Movement revealed regime internal divisions and popular discontent.

events.title: Severe Sanctions
events.description: The US and EU imposed unprecedented severe sanctions on Iran, targeting oil, banking, and shipping. Sanctions devastated Iran's economy; currency devalued, inflation soared. Iranian people suffered hardship, but the government maintained the nuclear program.

events.title: Rouhani Elected President
events.description: Moderate Hassan Rouhani was elected president, promising to resolve the nuclear issue and improve the economy. Rouhani engaged in dialogue with the West, seeking sanctions relief. His pragmatic foreign policy gained Supreme Leader Khamenei's support.

events.title: Iran Nuclear Deal Signed
events.description: Iran signed the comprehensive nuclear agreement (JCPOA) with six powers (US, UK, France, Russia, China, Germany). Iran limited its nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief. This was an Obama administration diplomatic achievement and Iran foreign policy victory, bringing hope for regional peace.

events.title: Economic Protests
events.description: Starting late 2017, Iran witnessed economic protests spreading to dozens of cities nationwide. Demonstrators protested high unemployment, inflation, and corruption, criticizing government foreign aid. The government suppressed protests, but economic discontent continued fermenting.

events.title: US Withdraws from Nuclear Deal
events.description: President Trump announced US withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal, reimposing 'maximum pressure' sanctions. This unilateral action destroyed the agreement, isolating America. Iran's economy plunged into crisis again, reformists setback, hardliners emboldened. US-Iran confrontation intensified.

events.title: Iran Withdraws from JCPOA Provisions
events.description: Under US sanctions pressure, Iran began gradually withdrawing from JCPOA restrictions, increasing uranium enrichment. Iran stated it would resume compliance if European countries fulfilled obligations. The nuclear crisis escalated again, Middle East tensions rose.

events.title: Gasoline Price Protests
events.description: Government sharply raised gasoline prices, triggering nationwide protests. Demonstrators burned banks, attacked government buildings. The government shut down the internet, violently suppressed protests; hundreds died. This was one of the bloodiest crackdowns since the Islamic Republic's establishment.

events.title: Soleimani Assassination
events.description: The US assassinated Iranian Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani with a drone in Baghdad. He was considered one of Iran's most powerful figures. Iran vowed revenge, attacking US bases in Iraq. US-Iran came to the brink of full war but ultimately showed restraint.

events.title: Ukrainian Plane Shootdown
events.description: Iran's Revolutionary Guards mistakenly shot down a Ukrainian passenger plane, killing all 176 aboard. The government initially denied responsibility but admitted error when faced with evidence. This tragedy triggered new protests; people were enraged at government lies and incompetence.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic
events.description: Iran became the Middle East's hardest-hit country; tens of thousands died. US sanctions hindered medical supply imports, exacerbating the crisis. The pandemic exposed Iran's healthcare system fragility and government mismanagement. The economy further deteriorated, people's suffering deepened.

events.title: Nuclear Scientist Fakhrizadeh Assassinated
events.description: Iran's chief nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh was assassinated in Tehran suburbs. Iran blamed Israel, vowing revenge. This assassination demonstrated Israel's operational capability inside Iran, highlighting Iran's security vulnerabilities.

events.title: Raisi Elected President
events.description: Hardliner judiciary chief Ebrahim Raisi was elected president with low turnout. Raisi was seen as Khamenei's successor; his election marked conservatives' complete control. Reformists were excluded from the political process; democratic space further narrowed.

events.title: Raisi Government Takes Office
events.description: Raisi government formed cabinet, all conservatives and hardliners. The government adopted more confrontational foreign policy but also sought to resume nuclear negotiations to lift sanctions. Domestically, social controls tightened, dissent suppressed.

events.title: Mahsa Amini's Death and Nationwide Protests
events.description: 22-year-old Mahsa Amini died after arrest by morality police for 'improper hijab,' sparking nationwide protests. The slogan 'Woman, Life, Freedom' echoed across Iran. Demonstrations lasted months, met with brutal crackdown, hundreds killed, thousands arrested. This was one of the gravest challenges to the Islamic Republic.

events.title: Iran-Saudi Normalization
events.description: Under Chinese mediation, Iran and Saudi Arabia restored diplomatic relations. The reconciliation of two regional arch-rivals shocked the world. This breakthrough could reduce Middle East tensions but faces many challenges. Iran used the diplomatic breakthrough to break isolation.

events.title: Nuclear Negotiations Deadlock
events.description: Negotiations to restore the JCPOA reached deadlock. Iran's uranium enrichment reached 60%, near weapons-grade. The IAEA warned of Iran's non-cooperation. The West threatened new sanctions but avoided military conflict. The nuclear issue remains one of the Middle East's greatest security challenges.

events.title: Continued Economic Hardship
events.description: US sanctions, corruption, mismanagement, and regional conflicts keep Iran's economy depressed. The rial devalues, inflation soars, unemployment rises. People's lives are difficult; discontent with the regime intensifies. The economic crisis is Iran's greatest challenge.

events.title: President Raisi Helicopter Crash
events.description: President Ebrahim Raisi and Foreign Minister died in a helicopter accident in East Azerbaijan Province. This sudden event shocked Iran, raising questions about succession and leadership stability. Supreme Leader Khamenei managed the situation, ensuring regime stability.
